en: Bun's file API
is essentially an alternative to the Node.js
file API, which Bun also supports.
So you can import the node-fs package, the
Node file system package, and it's built
into Bun. You don't need to install
anything. Here I'm importing the
promise-based version.
And in there you'll find things like
readFile. And that does what the name
implies, it reads a file. So why would you
not do that?
Well, you can, but Bun's native built-in
file API claims to be faster and more
optimized when executed with Bun. And I
mean, you need Bun to execute it because
it's not supported by Node, for example.
So when you're building a Bun application
where you know that you will execute it with
Bun, obviously, then if you wanna read a
file, you should strongly consider doing
that with Bun file, even though Node's
readFile function would work too because Bun
has that Node.js compatibility. But there's
no reason to fall back to Node.js if you
wanna read a file because Bun has the
built-in support for it. Now, Bun file takes
one main input and that's the path to the
file you wanna open
and then it gives you back an object with
various properties and methods. For example,
a name property, a size property which
contains the file size in bytes
but also a bunch of methods. For example, if
you wanna get the raw bytes, there is a
bytes method and that simply returns a
promise so you have to await it and then a
Uint8ArrayBuffer which contains the raw
bytes. There also is a text method if you
wanna read the input as raw text and get
back a string or a promise that resolves to
a string.
And then also other utility methods, for
example, for creating a stream if you wanna
stream in the file in chunks instead of
reading it as a whole into memory.
And also what we're using here, a JSON
method, and that gives us a promise that
will resolve to any, so to an object of any
shape. We don't know the shape in advance or
TypeScript doesn't know the shape in
advance, which is why I'm doing that
typecasting here to make it clear that once
we awaited this, we'll have an object of
this customer input shape.
Because what I'm reading in here are these
customer input files,
these JSON files here, which have JSON
objects in this format with ID, name, email,
and then items.
That's exactly the shape I'm describing here
with customer input.
So here I'm using Bunfile for reading that.
And of course, Bun does not just have a file
method for reading files, it also has a
method for writing files, the Bun.write
method.
And Bun.write may look complex here, but in
its simplest form, it also takes a path, a
string, and then the content that should be
written there.
But if we hover over it, we see it is a bit
more complex than that. The destination can
be
a path in the end.
It could also be a remote file on S3,
because Bun has a built-in S3 client and
I'll get back to that in a separate lecture.
And it could also be a handle to a file. So
we could open a file with bun file here
and then some path.
Of course, there should be a real path and
that file handle here could also be passed
here as an input so that you open a file,
you maybe read it and then you overwrite it
with bun write. That would work too. It's
not what I'm doing here, but you could do
that as well.
And then the input to the file can also be a
variety of things. It can be a string, which
is what HTML here in the end is. HTML is the
loaded invoice HTML
text in the end because HTML is just text
with those concrete values filled in. And
that string is then saved here with write
because a string is one of the supported
input values that are written into a file.
But you could also pass in raw bytes,
that are written to that file.
And you can also pass a 3rd object here
where you can also define whether a path
should be created.
So if you specify a path where the parent
directory is missing, if it should create
it, and by default this is true. So you
actually only need to set it if you don't
want Bun to create that path. So in case
that HTML path is not existing yet with
createPath false, you'd get an error instead
of bun creating it automatically.
And mode is simply the permission mode you
set on that file using that Linux octal
notation.
But here I don't need that because I'm fine
with the defaults.
And actually, even though bun would create
the path by default with bun write, I'm
ensuring the path exists here manually by
using mkdir.
So that creates the invoices output path if
it doesn't exist yet, and otherwise it just
ignores the existing file and does nothing.
Now mkdir, and that's why I'm adding it here
or why I have it here, is not coming from
Bun though, because Bun has those built-in
file APIs for writing and for reading, but
it does not have native built-in
folder operation APIs, if you wanna put it
like this. So an API for creating a
directory, for example, If you have an
application that needs to create a
directory, you could either rely on the
auto-creation functionality of Bun write if
it's coupled to writing a file, but if it's
not coupled to it, if you just wanna create
the directory, then you will need to use
Bun's Node.js compatibility and use the
Node.js mkdir function here because the Bun
file API is really only about reading with
Bun file and writing with Bun write. Those
APIs are flexible and pretty fast. And as
you see here, they're also super easy to
use.
